feat(interpreter): add the memory extension

A memory is a key and a body, and the body is either prose or a form.
One slot holds both because in a homoiconic language they are the same
material: the declarative and procedural halves of the issue are one
type, not two. memory/replay evaluates a form body by re-entering the
evaluator, so a remembered recipe becomes a running one.

Memories hook events through one grammar, a quoted (kind pattern):
call, result, error, step, prose, user and recall. The first three come
from an evalForm middleware that walks the whole form, so a call nested
in a setq still matches; the rest come from the MemoryBank the REPL
drives at its step boundary. Retrieval is itself an event, which is what
lets memories chain, and memories that fire together get wired together.

Firing is bounded and returned rather than emitted: a channel emission
after the eval would land in a dead subscription, and the compactor's
echo budget does not count anything that bypasses it. So the bank keeps
its own word budget and hands its text back at the step boundary.

Retrieval strengthens; silence decays on a half-life; under a floor a
memory is swept away. Retrieval also opens a plasticity window in which
memory/revise may correct the body, and the step closes it again.

The builtins are slashed because remember, recall and forget are
ordinary English verbs, and a bare one in an aside would stop being
prose and start being a call. memory/recall and memories join the
compactor's read forms so a retrieval prints itself instead of being
reported twice.

A Lisp promise is now the `Promise` object the MCP client produced, with no
wrapper of ours around it. `Job`, `Jobs`, `JobsRuntime`, `LocalJobsRuntime`, the

settles once and keeps its value, so awaiting twice needs no result cache. A
finalizer attached with `.then` runs exactly once whether or not anyone awaits,

settled (`promise-state` must not block, so the settling `.then` records

never awaits cannot kill the host on Node's unhandled-rejection.

feat(repl): name and truncate every result the REPL prints

MemoryRepl.eval is the choke point every model-facing consumer goes
through — apps/mcp passes its string to an MCP client verbatim and
packages/ai JSON-wraps it into the next turn — so capping here is enough
for both, and neither needs a change of its own.

Each top-level result is echoed as `name = value`, which is why the ~9
exact-string assertions in the existing suites move. That is the
intended behaviour change: the name is what lets a later step refer to
the value instead of re-emitting it.

Side-effect output is capped the same way and saved as `output-N`, since
a princ loop floods the window as effectively as a large return value.
It is buffered and measured once at the end rather than capped as it is
written. The interactive CLI caps only the value echo — it points the
interpreter's writer straight at stdout, so buffering to measure would
break streaming output, and a human at a terminal can scroll.

A program of several forms echoes only the last (the cap is per eval,
not per form) but every form still bound a name, so the others are
listed — otherwise the model cannot learn they exist short of (dump).

The Compressor is recreated per interpreter, the opposite of
secretsExtension's host-owned store: the naming counters must die with
the globals they named, or a reset() leaves the count climbing past
names that are no longer bound.

feat(interpreter): add context compression built-ins

The REPL is an LLM's only interface, so everything it prints is spent
context, and nothing bounded it: one (playwright/snapshot) or a 10k
element list could swallow the window in a single step. The only elision
in the printer was the circular-list guard in strListBody.

Two mechanisms that only work together. Every top-level result is bound
to a global named `<function>-<n>`, so the next step refers to
`linear/list-issues-1` instead of retyping the data — retyping is where
hallucinated ids and titles come from. And the printout is capped at a
word limit, closing with a `...` line naming the variable that holds the
rest. Truncating is only safe *because* of the naming: nothing is lost
by not printing it.

`view`/`head`/`tail`/`grep` read into a value. They take a value rather
than a handle, so `Compressor` holds no values at all — a named result is
an ordinary global, which means they work just as well on a `let`
binding or anything the agent named itself, and dump/doc need no
special-casing.

`grep` reports word offsets rather than line numbers because `str` of a
large list is a single line with no newlines in it: a line-oriented grep
would report one enormous match. A ±context-words window behaves the
same on a one-line Lisp render and on multi-line text, and the offset it
prints feeds straight back into `(view x :offset N)`.

A word cap alone bounds nothing — minified JSON is one megabyte-long
"word" — so MAX_CHARS_PER_WORD is a hard character backstop. A cut word
cannot be paged past by word offset, so its marker points at the
prelude's `substring` instead of `view`.

feat(telemetry): capture the browser half through a first-party proxy

The traces so far were only the server's side of the story. This adds the
browser's, through `@posthog/react`'s provider from the root route: pageviews,

can no longer recognise the region behind a proxied host.

turn produces carries `$session_id` and a run can be watched rather than only
read. It has to be named in the Hono CORS allowlist: leave it out and the
preflight rejects the chat itself, not just the telemetry that reads it.
